items.abstract: <jats:p>In contrast to the long-standing claim that Korolevo I is one of the oldest sites in Europe, dating to at least 1 Ma, the present author critically re-evaluates the site’s Lower Paleolithic record. This study presents an analysis of the site’s lower artifact-bearing sediments and lithic assemblages, highlighting problems with the stratigraphy and absolute dating, as well as the absence of genuine in situ artifacts. As a result, the only currently recognized Lower Paleolithic horizon at Korolevo I, Horizon VI, is dated to the mid–Middle Pleistocene, approximately 550 ka. The stratigraphic and artifact-related issues identified at Korolevo were assessed using previously established criteria and subsequently applied to several well-known Lower Paleolithic localities in Eastern Central Europe and the Balkans. In summary, as with Korolevo I, other briefly analyzed sites in these regions also lack evidence of true in situ lithic artifacts in Early Pleistocene sediments. Accordingly, the available data currently support the existence of only Middle Pleistocene Lower Paleolithic sites in Eastern Central Europe and the Balkans, raising the need to revise the timing of the initial hominin occupation of this part of the European continent during the Lower Paleolithic. Moreover, it is possible that the broader model of Europe’s initial peopling and subsequent hominin dispersal across the continent followed a west-to-east trajectory, beginning in the Iberian Peninsula around 1.3 Ma.</jats:p>

<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We provide descriptions and taphonomic and functional interpretations of two hominin clavicles, SWT1/HR‐5 and SWT1/HR‐6, from Swartkrans Member 1. We explore the possibility that one of the clavicles derives from the same
                      <jats:italic>Paranthropus robustus</jats:italic>
                      individual as SWT1/HR‐2, an articulating os coxae and partial lower limb from Swartkrans Member 1.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We employed taphonomic methods to describe damage on SWT1/HR‐5 and SWT1/HR‐6. Complementing the qualitative descriptions, we used osteometric tools and micro‐CT scanning to generate quantitative data on external shape, cross‐sectional geometry, and trabecular structure of the fossils. Observations were interpreted through comparative analyses. To explore a possible individual association of one of the new Swartkrans clavicles with the SWT1/HR‐2 fossil‐set, we developed linear regression models, fitted to extant hominoid samples. We then applied these models to each of the Swartkrans clavicles and to the SWT1/HR‐2b femur.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Periosteal surfaces of the Swartkrans clavicles retain important anatomical and taphonomic details. Their external shapes do not ally them exclusively with the clavicles of any comparative hominoid taxon. However, their cross‐sectional geometries and trabecular structures are ultimately consistent with apelike arboreality. Results fail to clarify whether the SWT1/HR‐5 and SWT1/HR‐6 individuals derived from the same taxon. Association of SWT1/HR‐2 with either clavicle could not be reliably determined, although such an association is more likely with SWT1/HR‐6.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The finding that SWT1/HR‐5 and SWT1/HR‐6 derived from arboreally active individuals concords with analyses of the SWT1/HR‐2 fossil‐set, strengthening the idea that arborealism was an important adaptation for some South African Pleistocene hominins.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
authors: Travis Rayne Pickering, Hannah N. Farrell, Jason L. Heaton, Kristian J. Carlson, Ronald J. Clarke, Matthew V. Caruana, Kathleen Kuman, Dominic Stratford, Marine Cazenave

items.abstract: Abstract The African Middle Stone Age (MSA) represents the cultural and technological context associated with the emergence of Homo sapiens and the development of complex cognition. In this setting, ochre use is considered a multifaceted proxy for modern behaviour, allowing inferences about technical and symbolic aspects of Homo sapiens. Powdered ochre is reported in multiple southern African ethnographic and archaeological contexts alongside various organic materials, some of which are protein-based. Yet, the recovery of proteinaceous residues is rare in the MSA. Since proteins can offer insights into their tissue and species of origin, identifying proteins in association with ochre may help to infer its function. At Klipdrift Shelter (South Africa), the 60 000-year-old Howiesons Poort layers contain a laterally continuous, ochre-rich sediment surface, possibly over 1 m long, 40 cm wide, and up to 1 cm thick. We used palaeoproteomics to identify proteinaceous traces from this feature. Our analysis identified type I collagen confidently matching common eland (Taurotragus oryx) in two samples. Together with the feature's highly complex nature, these findings suggest the deliberate mixing of eland-derived proteins with ochre powder. Our results confirm that palaeoproteomics can be a reliable tool for reconstructing the protein component of the early human material culture.

items.abstract: The accurate detection and classification of dental anomalies from radiographic images play a crucial role in modern dentistry for effective diagnosis and treatment planning. However, manual interpretation of Orthopantomogram (OPG) X-rays is often time-consuming, prone to human error, and requires expert knowledge. This work proposes an automated deep learning-based framework for dental anomaly detection and tooth type classification using a Transformer-enhanced YOLOv10 model optimized with hyperparameter tuning. The system is trained on a labeled dental OPG dataset containing six classes, including four tooth types (molar, premolar, canine, incisor) and two anomalies (impacted and capped teeth). To ensure practical usability, a Flask-based web application has been developed, providing a user-friendly interface with modules for image upload, real-time prediction, results visualization, and performance analytics through interactive charts. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high detection accuracy and robustness in identifying dental structures and anomalies. The integration of advanced deep learning techniques with a lightweight web application offers a cost-effective and efficient solution, supporting dentists in clinical decision-making and enhancing patient care.
